title: Master Class | Smith–Morra Gambit | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: Because the fianchetto setup doesn't immediately challenge the centre, there's no need to rush e6. Instead — exactly as in the Caro-Kann — develop the bishop to f5 first, getting it outside the pawn chain before the e-pawn shuts it in.
Only now does e6 go in, with the light-squared bishop already breathing free air outside the chain. It's an ideal, harmonious structure — everything developed to its best square.
A useful little move — h6 grants the bishop a bolt-hole on h7, so that any lunge at it with a knight to h4 is rendered completely harmless before it ever happens.

The knight to c3 is a familiar inaccuracy at this level — it blocks the c-pawn's path to c4, its most natural challenge to the centre. That leaves the centre as solid as it gets, with the c5 lever held in reserve.
Now castle — and note there's no real threat to the centre: it's defended three times while attacked only twice. Counting the guards against the attackers is what tells you a threat is empty.
And there's the knight lunge — which is precisely why the little luft move went in earlier. The bishop simply steps to h7, unbothered.

The central break is a genuine idea, opening things up. The plainest reply is to swap everything off on e4, which strips away the fianchetto bishop and leaves the enemy king a touch draughty — but there's a sharper sequence worth finding.

The cleverness rests on the fact that the recapturing knight is itself loose. Snap on e4, and after the recapture an in-between capture on h4 wrecks the opponent's pawns while staying a pawn ahead. Order the captures right and the extra material comes with a ruined enemy structure.

There's no obligation to capture on e4 at all — allowing a rook to sit there, ready to swing across for a kingside lift, is unpleasant. Since the bishop isn't truly threatened, a calm recapture keeps everything sound.
The Zen move is the knight to c6 — the tempting pawn advance would just blunder the rook. Same central idea, but a developing move instead of a loosening one.

For the small price of doubled pawns comes an opposite-coloured-bishop middlegame — and those famously favour the attacker, because the defender's bishop can never guard the squares under fire. The knight recapture even forks a pair of pawns as a bonus.
Now the window: the opponent's bishop still isn't out, so the king is under-defended. There's a small chance to strike — pry the centre open at any cost and the lagging development gets punished.

f5 is more forcing than the quieter break — it drives the rook off its square. If it retreats along the file the centre push wins; if it captures, a knight recapture hits it back with a discovered check lurking behind. Every branch keeps a threat attached.
The point that makes it work: the enemy queen is undefended, so the pawn can't be taken. That single loose piece is what powers the whole combination.
And this is exactly why speed matters — the moment the bishop finally develops, the queen is guarded, the discovered attack evaporates, and the tactics are gone. Urgency is the whole idea.
No need for anything fancy — bring the last rook into the game and set up an x-ray against the queen. Quietly improving the idle piece is what converts.

The knight jumps to b3, hitting the rook in the corner. And a safety check first — scan whether the enemy queen can reach a square that hits g7 for a mate threat; it can't, so the plan is clean. Always confirm the opponent has no counter-mate before committing.

The finish looks like a slip — a couple of pieces hang — but sharp vision reveals a forced mate. It begins with the rook, not the queen: if the knight is taken, the queen crashes into e4 for checkmate. Trust the calculation over the material count.

The one real moment was that knight-and-bishop combination — the correct defence would have been a knight to c5, counterattacking the queenside instead of grabbing. And a strategic note on the whole line: the c3 setup is risky, because if the central break never lands the opponent is simply left without a plan, while this side always keeps the c5 lever in hand.
